newsitem.title: BELARUS: Thousands march in Belarus despite Lukashenko ban.
newsitem.headline: Thousands march in Belarus despite Lukashenko ban.

text.p: Thousands of people defied a ban on marches in Belarus to protest against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and mark Constitution Day on Saturday.
"Long live Belarus!" they shouted, showing their opposition to plans for a union with neighbouring Russia which President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday could lead to a merger one day.
A Reuters correspondent on the scene said about 7,000 protesters had gathered by 11.30 (0930 GMT).
They moved along the pavements of the main street to a rally due to be held about two km (a mile and a half) away.
Authorities have given permission for the rally but specifically banned proceeding through the capital of the former Soviet republic on Russia's western border.
Opposition officials had vowed to go ahead with the march despite strong-arm tactics used by police to stop a similar rally taking place on Friday.

"We have seen that the authorities dealt with protesters in a very brutal manner. They want to frighten us," said Leonid Vasyuchenko, who was on duty at the headquarters of the opposition Popular Front on Friday night.
Police beat protesters and made about 50 arrests -- including two Germans, two Americans and several journalists -- at that meeting, attended mostly by young activists.
A leader of the Front was arrested on the eve of the protests in a late-night raid on the organisation's headquarters and charged with interfering with police work.
But on Saturday police let the crowd move along the street and there was no immediate sign they would break up the protest.
The rally was led by one of the country's most respected opposition figures, Semyon Sharetsky, speaker of parliament disbanded by Lukashenko after he won a referendum in November.
There was no sign of the red-and-white post-independence symbols banned by Lukashenko as part of a crackdown on the opposition, which has been promising him a "political spring".
Sharetsky led attempts to stop Lukashenko going ahead with the referendum, branded by critics as illegal.
Lukashenko is backed by most of the 10 million Belarussians but opposed by a loose union of liberals, nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly concentrated in Minsk.

The 42-year-old former farm boss used an overwhelming win to expand his authority over all branches of power, rewrite the constitution and restart his five-year term which began in 1994. He keeps a tight hold on the media, and the main television and radio channels are clearly pro-presidential. State-run television said on Friday that the Minsk police behaved in "a correct manner according to European standards".
Perhaps fearing scuffles near Lukashenko's residence, Minsk authorities announced repairs would be carried out on the stretch of the main street near the building on Saturday.
Some 60 deputies who refused to join the parliament set up under the new constitution met to call on the outside world not to recognise Lukashenko's new constitution.
The European Parliament still recognises the old parliament, saying the new one was formed illegally.

But Lukashenko praised his new constitution as a "guarantor of domestic political stability" in an address in official newspapers. "The updated constitution created a foundation for fulfilling the individual's rights and freedom," it said.
